analysis.one_liner: Opens SEC records about Wall Street firms to public records requests.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the SEC's new Dodd-Frank records-secrecy exemption died in committee with zero cosponsors and no action before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In July 2010, the Dodd-Frank financial law added a provision shielding records the SEC obtains from Wall Street firms — trading data collected for surveillance and risk assessment — from public records requests. H.R. 6086, introduced in August 2010, would have repealed that shield, amending the securities laws so the SEC's records about registered firms could be obtained under the Freedom of Information Act. The bill sat in two House committees with no cosponsors and no action, and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, journalists, researchers, investors, and the public could have filed public records requests for SEC records about registered Wall Street firms — including trading data the SEC collects for surveillance and risk assessment — instead of being refused under the Dodd-Frank exemption.

how_it_helps.text: It would amend the Securities Exchange Act to strike the Dodd-Frank prohibition on compelling the SEC to disclose records obtained from registered persons during its regulatory and oversight activities.

It would make the same change in parallel provisions of the Investment Company Act and Investment Advisers Act, repealing similar bans on disclosing records provided by investment companies, advisers, and majority-owned broker-dealer or adviser subsidiaries used for surveillance and risk assessment.

It declares the SEC a financial-regulator agency for FOIA purposes while retaining the standard exemption for examination reports, meaning general SEC records could be requested but statutory examination reports would stay exempt.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, registered firms — hedge funds, broker-dealers, investment companies, and investment advisers — would have borne the cost: records they provide to the SEC, including trading data gathered for surveillance, could have been disclosed on request rather than kept confidential.

drawbacks.text: The Dodd-Frank provision the bill would repeal was written to keep records obtained from registered firms — including trading data gathered for surveillance — out of public records requests, on the theory that firms and their counterparties could be harmed if confidential positions and dealings were exposed.

The bill retains the general FOIA exemption for examination, operating, or condition reports prepared by or for the SEC, so its effect would be narrower than full openness — but firms submitting information to the SEC for surveillance and risk assessment would still lose the specific shield Dodd-Frank had just given them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: sunshine over the SEC's surveillance of Wall Street, with no direct cost to ordinary taxpayers. The cost falls on regulated firms, whose trading records provided to the SEC could be released under the public records law rather than kept confidential. Honest supporters would acknowledge a genuine design concern: the bill would have exposed information firms hand over in examinations, which critics of the Dodd-Frank exemption's repeal argued could be used by competitors or tip off market participants. The bill did soften this by keeping the general FOIA exemption for examination reports, but it did not resolve the underlying confidentiality question, and with no cosponsors it never received the scrutiny that question deserved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to the Financial Services Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee on August 10, 2010, the day it was introduced, and the record shows no further action of any kind.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired with the Congress without ever being voted on.
As a result, the Dodd-Frank provision blocking public records requests for SEC records about registered firms remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms that provide records to the SEC were better off: the Dodd-Frank exemption shielding their records from public records requests stayed on the books untouched, and no one gained access to the data.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street firms whose SEC records stay sealed

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.role: Chair, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the SEC's new FOIA exemption and referred it to two House committees.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is recorded anywhere in the bill's history; the simply bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party and died in committee.

industries.industry: Registered financial firms (hedge funds, broker-dealers, investment companies and advisers)
industries.note: The bill would strip the just-enacted shield that kept records these firms provide to the SEC for surveillance and risk assessment out of public records requests. Their positions and dealings known to the regulator could be disclosed on request. The industry's interest in keeping this data confidential runs against the public's interest in seeing how the regulator oversees it.

industries.industry: News media, researchers, and transparency advocates
industries.note: Repealing the exemption would let journalists and the public file FOIA requests for SEC records about Wall Street firms rather than being flatly refused. The bill died before any of this could happen.
